prompt:
Calculate the usable memory and price efficiency for each cache node type in the price sheet. The cache engine reserves 25 percent of advertised memory for indexes, runtime state, and compaction.

First, compute the usable memory for each node after applying the 25 percent engine overhead. Then calculate the monthly price per usable gigabyte for each node type. Present the results in a clear table at docs/memory-table.md.

Use the price-sheet.json file for the raw node data and the operating-model.md for the engine reservation percentage. The table should include columns for node ID, advertised memory, usable memory after overhead, monthly price, and price per usable GB. Round monetary values to two decimal places and memory values to one decimal place.

This is a straightforward calculation task that requires no design decisions or recommendations.

checks.cmd: cp hidden/meta.json meta.json && mkdir -p fixture && cp -r hidden/_pristine/. fixture/ && ( [ -L solution ] || [ ! -e solution ] || mv solution .bench-agent-solution ) && ln -sfn . solution && node --test hidden/*.test.js

rubric.criterion: All calculated values (usable memory, price per GB) are mathematically correct within 1% tolerance, derived from the fixture data. Fail: usable memory is not 75% of advertised, or price per GB divides by advertised memory, or the values are copied rather than computed. Partial: most rows are right within 1% but one or two nodes are wrong, or the 25% overhead is applied inconsistently. Pass: every node in price-sheet.json (taken from the JSON, not the markdown sheet) shows usable = 0.75 x advertised, price per usable GB = monthly price / usable memory, within 1%, and cache-105 comes out as the cheapest at about 8.25 USD per usable GB. (not code-checkable: The test suite already verifies numerical accuracy, so this rubric item ensures the agent didn't hardcode answers but performed the calculations correctly from source data.)

The table is clearly formatted with appropriate column headers, consistent rounding (memory to 1 decimal, prices to 2 decimals), and includes explanatory notes about the calculations. Fail: no table, or it lacks the five requested columns (node ID, advertised memory, usable memory, monthly price, price per usable GB). Partial: all five columns exist but rounding is inconsistent (memory to one decimal, money to two) or there is no note on the method. Pass: a clean table with the five columns and the requested rounding, a short note citing operating-model.md for the 25% reservation, written to docs/memory-table.md, with no recommendation, no use of candidate-configs.json or the 118 GB working set, and no ADR file. (not code-checkable: While tests check basic formatting, human judgment is needed to assess whether the presentation is clear, well-organized, and includes helpful explanatory context beyond the raw numbers.)

verdicts.note: The prompt describes the calculation method (25% overhead) but does not name frameworks, libraries, or hint at specific answers beyond the arithmetic itself.
The 25% reservation is stated clearly in both the prompt and operating-model.md; rounding rules are explicit (memory 1 decimal, prices 2 decimals); file locations are unambiguous.
Fixture files provide raw data and parameters but do not contain pre-calculated answers or the final table.
The task requires parsing JSON, extracting a percentage from markdown, applying the formula, and formatting a table with correct rounding - substantive work beyond picking the cheapest option.
All required inputs are present: price-sheet.json has node data, operating-model.md has the 25% reservation; the prompt specifies output location and rounding rules.
